newsitem.title: UK: British doctors cite new test for viral infections.
newsitem.headline: British doctors cite new test for viral infections.

text.p: British doctors said on Friday that a laboratory DNA test could be the most valuable method for detecting diseases that are notoriously difficult to diagnose, such as viral meningitis and encephalitis.

They used a process called polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify minute quantities of DNA -- deoxyribonucleic acid, the self-replicating material present in nearly all living organisms -- to help them detect viral infections of the central nervous system.

Writing in The Lancet medical journal, they said they tested for the most common viruses -- enteroviruses, herpes simplex virus, Epstein-Barr virus and varicella zoster viruses -- and concluded that a patient with a positive PCR test was almost 90 times as likely to have a viral infection of the central nervous system as not.
Because there is no existing test which can say definitely whether a patient has one of these viral infections, the doctors findings were difficult to verify.

So they divided more than 400 patients into groups that had been clinically defined as definitely, probably or possibly having a viral infection of the central nervous system and a fourth group which was not thought to be infected.
Then they set the PCR results against the clinical diagnoses.
"A negative PCR result can be used with moderate confidence to rule out a diagnosis of the viral infection of the central nervous system," the doctors said.
"We believe that PCR will become the first-line diagnostic test for viral meningitis and encephalitis -- the most common types of of central nervous system infections."
